articleBody:
Miami's bar landscape is shifting as a new wave of establishments brings vermouth and sherry to the forefront of the city's cocktail consciousness. According to Eater Miami, these new venues are reshaping how the city approaches mixed drinks, layering Spanish and Italian traditions onto the foundation of rum and agave spirits that have long defined Miami's drinking culture.

As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has historically excelled at channeling diverse flavors—rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Now, vermouth and sherry-based cocktails, along with classic Spanish drinks, are becoming central to this equation. Vermouth, an aromatized fortified wine flavored with various botanicals, was first produced in its modern form during the mid- to late 18th century in Turin, Italy, before becoming a staple of European cocktail culture. Sherry, a fortified wine produced from white grapes around the city of Jerez de la Frontera in Andalusia, Spain, offers its own range of styles—from light, delicate versions like Manzanilla and fino to darker, more complex expressions such as Amontillado and oloroso that have oxidized over years in barrel.

These new bars are not simply importing European cocktail templates but rather synthesizing them with Miami's established spirits heritage. The vermouth and sherry boom reflects a broader professional maturation within Miami's hospitality community, where bartenders and owners are drawing on centuries of European tradition while maintaining the tropical and Latin American flavors that distinguish the city's unique position.

For consumers, the expansion offers a chance to explore cocktails that bridge continents and centuries. The bars signal that Miami's drinking culture is evolving beyond its historical identity, creating space for sophisticated, layered beverages that honor multiple traditions. Whether vermouth-forward aperitivos or sherry-based cocktails, these new establishments are demonstrating that Miami's role as a cultural nexus extends naturally to its bar programs, where Old World techniques meet New World ingredients and sensibilities.

whatHappening: Miami Spice Restaurant Month is returning for its 25th edition, running from August 1 through September 30, 2026. The program now features a new reserve tier and will include more than 300 participating restaurants offering three-course prix-fixe menus at minimum 30% savings.
whoInvolved: The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau (GMCVB) is organizing the event. The GMCVB is the official destination marketing organization for the Miami area, responsible for promoting tourism and hospitality initiatives throughout the region.
whyMatters: Miami Spice has become a signature dining event that drives significant traffic to local restaurants during the slower summer months, benefiting both the hospitality industry and diners seeking quality meals at reduced prices. The expansion to over 300 restaurants and the introduction of a reserve tier signals the program's growing prominence as a major culinary event that strengthens Miami's reputation as a world-class dining destination.
articleBody:
The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau has announced the return of Miami Spice Restaurant Month, marking the 25th year of the popular culinary initiative. Running from August 1 through September 30, 2026, the program will feature three-course prix-fixe menus at participating establishments, with diners saving a minimum of 30% on their meals. According to Miami Curated, the expanded edition will include more than 300 restaurants, representing significant growth from previous years.

This year's iteration introduces a new reserve tier to the program, though specific details about how this premium category will function remain limited. The addition suggests the GMCVB is working to segment the dining experience, potentially offering different price points or exclusive access levels to accommodate restaurants and diners at various market positions. The reserve tier may appeal to high-end establishments seeking to participate while maintaining brand positioning.

Miami Spice has long served as a strategic initiative to boost restaurant traffic during the summer months, traditionally a slower period for dining in South Florida. By offering substantial discounts, the program encourages both locals and tourists to explore new venues and support the hospitality sector during a season when many residents leave the area due to heat and humidity. The program's longevity—now in its second quarter-century—demonstrates its success in achieving these goals.

The expansion to over 300 participating restaurants underscores the program's reach across Miami's diverse culinary landscape. This scale allows diners to select from establishments spanning various cuisines, price ranges, and neighborhoods, making the initiative accessible to a broad audience. The minimum 30% savings requirement ensures genuine value for participants, distinguishing Miami Spice from typical restaurant promotions.

For the broader Miami dining community, the program remains a cornerstone event in the annual calendar. Restaurants view participation as an opportunity to introduce their menus to new customers, while the GMCVB leverages the initiative to reinforce Miami's status as a major culinary destination. With the 25th edition approaching, the program continues to evolve while maintaining its core mission of connecting diners with quality restaurants at exceptional prices.

title: Where Elegance Lives: 5 Wonderful Miami Bars
summary: One of my go-to spots when I’m in New York City is the iconic King Cole Bar at the St. Regis. Stepping inside always feels like an immersion into a bygone era—a time when elegance was a deeply desired way of life. Even as modern fashion has shifted toward the casual, the bar…
whatHappening: A Miami-focused bar guide highlights five establishments that prioritize elegance and sophistication. The piece draws parallels to iconic venues like the King Cole Bar at Manhattan's St. Regis, celebrating bars that maintain a commitment to refined aesthetics in an increasingly casual world.
whoInvolved: Miami Curated, a lifestyle publication covering the Miami area, is the source. The article references the King Cole Bar at the St. Regis New York, a legendary luxury hotel bar that has operated since the hotel's 1904 completion by developer John Jacob Astor IV.
whyMatters: The article speaks to a broader cultural tension: as fashion and social norms have trended casual, some venues continue to champion elegance and formality as deliberate lifestyle choices. For travelers and locals seeking refined experiences, curated guides to sophisticated bars offer an alternative to the dominant casual-dining culture.
articleBody:
The author of this Miami bar guide has long appreciated the timeless allure of iconic cocktail lounges. One such favorite is the King Cole Bar at the St. Regis in Manhattan, where stepping inside transports visitors to an earlier era when elegance was prized as a fundamental way of life. The bar's enduring appeal lies in its refusal to abandon refined sensibilities, even as contemporary fashion and social customs have moved decidedly toward the casual and informal.

The St. Regis New York, completed in 1904 and designed by the architectural firm Trowbridge & Livingston, was originally developed by John Jacob Astor IV. Today, the hotel is operated by Marriott International and maintains both Forbes five-star and AAA five-diamond ratings. The King Cole Bar has become synonymous with the luxury hotel experience, embodying the standards of sophistication that defined early-twentieth-century hospitality.

According to Miami Curated, the same commitment to elegance can be found in Miami's bar scene, where five establishments stand out for their refined approach to cocktails and ambiance. These venues share a philosophical alignment with spaces like the King Cole Bar—they reject the notion that modern life requires abandoning dress codes, classical décor, or the rituals associated with old-world hospitality.

The tension between formal and casual has reshaped the hospitality industry over decades. Yet certain bars have become refuges for those who value the ceremonial aspects of drinking culture. They maintain dress codes, hire skilled bartenders steeped in classic cocktail technique, and invest in interior design that evokes particular historical periods or aesthetic traditions. In doing so, they serve patrons seeking an experience that feels distinct from everyday casual dining and drinking.

For travelers and locals alike, discovering bars that prioritize elegance offers a counterpoint to ubiquitous casual venues. Miami's bar landscape increasingly includes such establishments, venues where the commitment to refinement remains uncompromised by broader cultural shifts. The guide serves as a curated roadmap for those who, like the author, believe that elegance remains a worthwhile aspiration in contemporary social life.

title: Eating News in Miami, July 2026
summary: A different kind of tea time -- tipsy tea, an unbeatable offer for mango lovers, new high profile restaurant in Coral Gables, ladies night with all the perks, a new waterfront option for cocktails and delicious comfort food from leading chefs, decadent ice cream and churros,…
whatHappening: Miami's dining scene is heating up this July 2026 with a wave of new and trending food and beverage experiences. From tipsy tea events to new high-profile restaurants opening in Coral Gables and waterfront cocktail bars, the city is offering everything from ladies' nights to artisanal desserts crafted by leading chefs.
whoInvolved: Miami's hospitality and culinary community is driving these trends, including established restaurant groups, independent chefs, and venue operators across neighborhoods like Coral Gables and the waterfront districts. These establishments are competing to capture the city's growing appetite for experiential dining and social food events.
whyMatters: The proliferation of themed dining experiences and new restaurant openings reflects Miami's position as a major food and entertainment destination, signaling strong consumer spending and confidence in the hospitality sector. These venues also indicate a shift toward more casual, social dining experiences that blend food, drink, and entertainment—a trend that shapes how restaurants compete for Miami's diners.
articleBody:
Miami's food and beverage landscape is undergoing a summer transformation, with restaurants and bars launching creative new concepts designed to appeal to locals and tourists alike. According to Miami Curated, July 2026 is shaping up to be a banner month for dining innovation, with everything from tipsy tea gatherings to mango-focused promotions and new waterfront cocktail destinations emerging across the city.

The diversity of offerings reflects how competitive the Miami dining market has become. High-profile new restaurants in Coral Gables are joining existing establishments in vying for attention, while themed events like ladies' nights with special perks are designed to drive traffic on traditionally slower evenings. Mango lovers are finding particular reason to celebrate, with at least one establishment rolling out promotions around the beloved tropical fruit—a fitting focus in a region where fresh produce plays a central role in the culinary identity.

Beyond the savory offerings, Miami's dessert scene is also experiencing a creative surge. Artisanal ice cream and churro offerings from established chefs are elevating what might traditionally be considered simple indulgences into destination-worthy treats. The presence of leading chefs in the dessert space underscores how seriously the city's food community is taking the entire dining experience, from cocktails to final course.

The waterfront has become particularly active, with new cocktail bars and venues offering both drinks and comfort food catering to Miami's growing population of diners seeking social experiences. These establishments capitalize on the city's natural assets while competing with established hospitality brands for market share.

Together, these developments suggest a market confident enough to support experimentation and willing to seek out novel dining experiences. For Miami's hospitality industry, the summer surge represents both opportunity and the necessity to differentiate in an increasingly crowded marketplace.

title: From Casual Lunch to Serious Dinner: Paperfish Sushi Brickell Stepped Up Its Game
summary: Paperfish Sushi Brickell has always been one of my “go to” places to have lunch or happy hour with a friend and they always like it. With all of the sushi restaurants in town you’d ask why Paperfish Sushi? The lovely décor that brightens up your day the moment you walk in,…
whatHappening: Paperfish Sushi Brickell has elevated its offerings beyond casual lunch and happy hour, stepping up to become a serious dining destination. The restaurant is leveraging its existing appeal—stylish décor and consistent quality—to compete more aggressively in Miami's crowded sushi market.
whoInvolved: Paperfish Sushi Brickell is a sushi restaurant operating in Brickell, Miami's financial district neighborhood. The establishment has built a loyal customer base through casual dining and after-work social gatherings before expanding its ambitions.
whyMatters: The restaurant's evolution reflects a broader competitive dynamic in the local dining scene, where casual neighborhood spots must differentiate or risk being overshadowed by newer competitors. For diners, the upgrade signals expanded dining options in Brickell's commercial center, which historically anchors the South Florida region's business community.
articleBody:
Paperfish Sushi Brickell, a fixture in Miami's financial district, is making a deliberate push to shed its image as merely a lunch-and-happy-hour spot, positioning itself instead as a destination for serious dinner experiences. The restaurant's strategy centers on amplifying the qualities that already attracted regulars—thoughtful interior design and consistent quality—while signaling a commitment to elevated service and ambition.

The Brickell neighborhood, located directly east of Interstate 95 and directly south of downtown Miami's Central Business District, serves as the financial hub for Miami and the broader South Florida region. Within this competitive marketplace, casual dining establishments face relentless pressure from both new concepts and established competitors vying for the same clientele. According to Miami Curated, Paperfish Sushi has always been a reliable choice for professionals seeking a low-key meal or social gathering, but the restaurant's owners appear to recognize that consistency alone is insufficient in a market saturated with sushi options.

What sets Paperfish apart, according to the venue's loyal patrons, is the aesthetic experience. The restaurant's décor creates an inviting atmosphere that immediately changes the mood upon entry—a detail often overlooked but crucial to the dining experience. In a downtown financial district where many restaurants operate on volume and transience, this attention to environment provides psychological separation from the typical business lunch.

The transition from casual to serious dining represents more than cosmetic adjustment. It signals a strategic decision to capture higher-ticket spending occasions, likely dinner service for groups and business clients entertaining clients or celebrating milestones. By maintaining its appealing design language while strengthening its dinner program, Paperfish avoids the trap of competing solely on price or novelty.

For the Brickell community, the restaurant's ambitions matter because they reflect the neighborhood's evolving character. As a financial district, Brickell attracts professionals who value both efficiency during lunch hours and quality experiences during dinner hours. A restaurant that successfully bridges both occasions becomes a more integrated part of the neighborhood's social and professional fabric.

whoInvolved: Dolce & Gabbana, the Italian luxury fashion house founded in 1985, recently hosted a major show in Miami that drew crowds to the area. whyMatters: New openings in the Miami Design District signal continued investment and growth in one of South Florida's premier shopping destinations, particularly as tourism rebounds post-event season. articleBody:
The Miami Design District is capitalizing on a post-event lull to highlight its expanding roster of shops and restaurants. With the crowds from the Dolce & Gabbana fashion show and FIFA activities having dispersed, according to Miami Curated, now represents an ideal window for visitors to explore the neighborhood's newest offerings without the typical surge of event-driven foot traffic.

The Miami Design District has long established itself as a premier destination in Florida, housing over 130 art galleries, showrooms, creative services firms, architecture offices, luxury fashion stores, antique dealers, eateries and bars. This concentration of retail, dining, and cultural venues has made the neighborhood a magnet for both tourists and discerning local shoppers seeking curated experiences beyond typical mall environments.

The timing of new store and restaurant openings carries particular significance. Major fashion events like the Dolce & Gabbana shows attract substantial crowds and media attention, temporarily transforming the district's character. Once those events conclude, the neighborhood settles into a more manageable rhythm—one where new establishments can introduce themselves to audiences without competing for attention against headline-grabbing runway shows or international sporting events.

The new openings reportedly include brands that may be unfamiliar to many shoppers, suggesting the district is continuing to diversify its merchant mix beyond established luxury names. This strategy positions the Miami Design District as a place of discovery rather than a destination where shoppers simply visit known anchors.

For visitors planning trips to Miami, the current moment presents a practical advantage. The combination of newly available shopping and dining experiences, coupled with reduced event-driven congestion, creates conditions for a more leisurely and personalized exploration of what the neighborhood has to offer. The district's existing infrastructure of galleries, showrooms, and cultural spaces provides context and variety that extends beyond shopping alone.

title: PASTA: The Model Miami Restaurant
summary: Very reasonable prices, excellent food across the board, very good service, low noise decibel so you can easily talk, PASTA is a dream restaurant which should serve as a model to others in Miami. I'll even go so far as to say it has the best pasta in Miami. And on top of all…
whatHappening: PASTA, a Miami restaurant, is earning widespread acclaim for delivering exceptional food quality, attentive service, and a comfortable dining atmosphere at accessible prices. The establishment has become a standout model for how restaurants in the competitive Miami dining scene should operate.
whoInvolved: PASTA is a pasta-focused restaurant operating in Miami, Florida. The venue has gained recognition through Miami Curated, a local dining and culture publication that reviews and recommends notable restaurants and establishments in the Miami area.
whyMatters: In a market often dominated by high-priced establishments with inconsistent execution, PASTA demonstrates that restaurants can succeed by prioritizing fundamentals: quality ingredients, skilled preparation, reasonable pricing, and genuine hospitality. Its success challenges the notion that Miami dining requires premium pricing or pretension, offering a template that other restaurateurs could emulate to better serve their communities.
articleBody:
A Miami restaurant is drawing attention for what it does best: serving excellent pasta in an unpretentious, welcoming environment. PASTA has emerged as a standout establishment in a city where dining venues often prioritize atmosphere and price point over straightforward quality and value.

According to Miami Curated, the restaurant excels across multiple dimensions that typically operate in tension at other establishments. The kitchen maintains high standards for its pasta dishes while keeping prices at levels accessible to regular diners, not just special-occasion crowds. The service staff demonstrates attentiveness without hovering, and the dining room maintains a noise level conducive to conversation—a feature notably absent from many trendy Miami restaurants where decibel levels often inhibit meaningful interaction among guests.

The restaurant's approach suggests a deliberate philosophy: mastery of core competencies rather than diversification or spectacle. By focusing on pasta preparation, PASTA has developed expertise that reviewers describe as best-in-class for the Miami market. The consistency of execution across the menu indicates a kitchen with clear standards and the discipline to maintain them nightly.

The model PASTA represents carries implications for Miami's broader dining landscape. High-end restaurants often justify premium pricing through elaborate service rituals, imported ingredients, or architectural drama. Mid-market establishments frequently compete on concept novelty rather than culinary excellence. PASTA's success suggests appetite among Miami diners for restaurants that prioritize fundamental hospitality and skilled execution over trend-chasing or unnecessary complexity.

The establishment's reasonable pricing structure deserves particular attention in a market where similar-quality dining typically commands significantly higher tabs. By controlling costs without compromising ingredient quality or technique, PASTA has created a sustainable model that can be profitable while remaining accessible. This challenges the assumption, sometimes implicit in upscale dining, that excellence requires corresponding expense to the customer.

Restaurants aspiring to similar standing would do well to study PASTA's execution: the discipline to focus on mastery of a defined cuisine, the operational competence to deliver consistent quality nightly, the service training that balances attentiveness with discretion, and the pricing discipline that values long-term loyalty over maximum per-table revenue. In a market that often rewards novelty and noise, PASTA's quiet excellence stands as a compelling counterargument.
